Home prices by ZIP: a hierarchical model, metro by metro

Code 
source("R/functions.R")
cfg$use_coast <- isTRUE(params$use_coast)
load_packages(geo = params$mode == "listings")
dat <- load_or_build(cfg, params$mode, rebuild = isTRUE(params$rebuild))
d <- prep_sales(dat$sales, cfg)
keys <- levels(d$metro)
ref <- keys[1]
fmt_pct <- function(x, d = 0) sprintf(paste0("%+.", d, "f%%"), x)
locals <- lapply(stats::setNames(keys, keys), function(k) run_local(d, k))
cmp <- if (length(keys) > 1) run_comparison(d)

Design

This report covers St. Louis and Orange County: 75,642 homes sold between October 2024 and October 2026.

Each metro is first analyzed on its own, then the metros are compared in a pooled model at the end. Two questions run through both parts: how much is a given house worth in each place, and how much of the price variation comes from where (ZIP, school district) rather than what (size, rooms, age, HOA)?

Local model (one per metro). Sales are nested in ZIP codes. School districts cut across ZIPs, so they enter as a crossed random effect, not a nested one:

\[ \log P_i = \mathbf{x}_i'\boldsymbol\beta + \mathbf{w}_{z[i]}'\boldsymbol\gamma + \tau_{q[i]} + u_{z[i]} + v_{s[i]} + \varepsilon_i, \qquad u \sim N(0,\sigma^2_{zip}),\; v \sim N(0,\sigma^2_{district}) \]

  • \(\mathbf{x}_i\) is the house: log sqft, beds, baths, age (quadratic), property type, an HOA indicator and log HOA fee.
  • \(\mathbf{w}_z\) is the location: the effective property-tax rate (ACS) and, for coastal metros, log distance to the coast.
  • \(\tau_q\) are sale-quarter effects; \(u\) and \(v\) are the ZIP and school-district intercepts.

Comparison model (pooled). All metros are fit together, adding predictors in blocks, a classic hierarchical regression, with metro-specific variances and slopes added last. The first metro, St. Louis, is the reference.

Note

\(P\) is the list price, not the sale price. Missouri is a non-disclosure state, so sold prices are missing for every St. Louis sale in the listing data. List price is used everywhere so metros stay comparable. Where a metro does have sold prices, its section checks how far list sits from sold.

Data

  • Sales: sold homes from Realtor.com (via homeharvest), single-family, condo and townhome only. Prices outside $50k–$20M, sizes outside 300–15,000 sqft, and the top and bottom 1% of $/sqft in each metro are dropped.
  • School districts: Census TIGER boundaries. Where an area has separate elementary and high-school districts, the pair is the district.
  • Tax rate: ACS 5-year, aggregate real-estate taxes divided by aggregate home value, by ZIP.
  • Coast: distance from each home to the TIGER coastline, for metros with a coast configured.

St. Louis

40,392 sales in 86 ZIPs and 45 school districts. After the house controls, 64% of the remaining price variation sits at the ZIP and school-district level. A 10% larger house lists for about 5.3% more. The top ZIP after controls is 63105 (Clayton) at +107%.

List vs. sold price

Orange County has sold prices as well as list prices, so it shows how much using list price matters. The median sale closes at 99.7% of list; across list-price quartiles the median ratio runs from 0.980 to 1.000. Fitting the same local model to sold price instead, ZIP premiums correlate with the list-price ones at r = 0.997, and the largest coefficient shift is 0.014 log points (Tax rate (+1 pt)).

Comparison across metros

Sample

Code

Blockwise model sequence

All blocks are fit by maximum likelihood on the same sample, so log-likelihoods, AIC and likelihood-ratio tests are comparable. For OLS blocks \(R^2_m = R^2_c\) is the ordinary \(R^2\). For mixed blocks they are Nakagawa’s marginal (fixed effects only) and conditional (fixed plus random) \(R^2\).

House features are centered at pooled means and sale quarter uses sum-to-zero contrasts, so each metro coefficient is the log-price gap versus St. Louis for a single-family home with no HOA, at the pooled average size, beds, baths and age, averaged across quarters, at each metro’s typical tax rate and coast distance. Property type and HOA shift every metro equally until block B7, which lets the HOA effect differ by metro.

Code

  dplyr::mutate(txt = sprintf("%s [%s, %s]", fmt_pct(gap_pct), fmt_pct(gap_lo), fmt_pct(gap_hi)),
                metro = paste(metro_labels[metro], "premium")) |>
  dplyr::select(block, metro, txt) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = metro, values_from = txt)

Cross-check: ZIP-level model on public ACS data

This model uses only Census data, one row per ZCTA. The outcome is log median owner-reported home value. Controls are median rooms, the share of homes with 4+ bedrooms, median year built, the tax rate and coastal distance, with school-district intercepts. Rows are weighted by owner-occupied units. It needs no listing data, but it describes the housing stock, not recent sales. ACS top-codes median value at $2M, which compresses the richest ZIPs.

Code 
z <- prep_zips(dat$zips, cfg)
zfit <- fit_zip_models(z)
modelsummary::modelsummary(list(`OLS (weighted)` = zfit$ols, `Multilevel` = zfit$mlm),
                           stars = TRUE, fmt = 3, gof_map = c("nobs", "aic"))

Caveats

  • List price. Metros without sold prices can’t be checked directly. A metro whose homes close further below list than another’s would make the gap between them look a point or two larger than it is. Redfin’s metro sale-to-list ratios are an easy outside check.
  • Tax rates. The ACS effective rate is taxes paid divided by self-reported value. Under Prop 13, long-time California owners pay far below 1% of market value, so there the rate mostly measures owner tenure plus Mello-Roos and other special assessments, not the rate a buyer faces. That is why it is centered within each metro.
  • HOA. A missing fee is coded as no HOA. HOA status is tangled with property type and amenities, so read it as an association, not the causal price of an HOA.
  • School districts enter as intercepts, which absorb quality without naming it. A district test-score measure (for example SEDA) as a level-2 predictor would make that explicit.
  • Selection. Sold homes are not a random sample of the stock, and metros have different stock mixes. Pooled centering means the reference house is more typical of some ZIPs than others.
  • Fit. R² values are in-sample, with no holdout validation. Residual variance differs by metro, which the pooled model doesn’t allow for.
  • Retransformation. Predictions are exp(mean log), roughly a median. Multiply by \(e^{\hat\sigma^2/2}\) for a mean.

Adding a metro

Add an entry to cfg$metros in R/functions.R, then refetch and rerun. The new metro gets its own section here and joins the comparison automatically:

DEN = list(
  label = "Denver", state = "CO",
  counties = c("08031", "08005", "08059"),   # county FIPS codes
  zcta_prefix = c("800", "801", "802")       # ZIP prefixes to search
  # coast = "Pacific"                        # only for coastal metros
)
